proposedTopics.title: Token Standards
proposedTopics.description: The ERC token interfaces every dApp speaks: ERC-20 (fungible), ERC-721 (non-fungible), ERC-1155 (multi-token), ERC-4626 (tokenized vaults), and ERC-165 interface detection. Standardization is what lets wallets, DEXes, and marketplaces integrate a token they've never seen.

proposedTopics.title: Proxies & Upgradeability
proposedTopics.description: How to ship a fixable contract on an immutable chain: a proxy holds state and delegatecalls logic, so the logic address can be swapped. Covers Transparent, UUPS, Beacon and Diamond patterns, ERC-1967 slots, the initializer discipline, and the storage-collision minefield they all share.

proposedTopics.title: Access Control Patterns
proposedTopics.description: Who is allowed to call privileged functions: single-owner (Ownable), role-based (AccessControl), and two-step ownership handoff. Getting this wrong — a missing modifier or an owner set to the wrong address — is the most common critical finding in real audits.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-20 fungible token standard
proposedTopics.description: ERC-20 defines fungible tokens through six required methods — totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, transferFrom, approve, allowance — plus Transfer/Approval events and three optional metadata methods. Every DEX, lending market, and wallet integrates against this shape. The standard specifies bool returns for transfer operations, but some deployed tokens return no value, so a typed IERC20 call can fail while SafeERC20 handles a non-reverting empty return.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Token.sol extending OpenZeppelin ERC20 with an initial mint, plus test/phase04/Token.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves transfer moves balances, emits Transfer, and reverts on insufficient balance. Threat: fee-on-transfer / rebasing tokens (amount received != amount sent), missing-return non-compliant tokens, and the approval race — never assume a token is well-behaved.

requirements.purpose: Implement and test the required fungible-token transfer and allowance interface

options.title: ERC-20: Token Standard
options.why: The canonical final ERC distinguishes six required methods, optional metadata, boolean transfer returns, zero-value transfers, and event requirements used by the build.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-20 approvals & SafeERC20
proposedTopics.description: approve + transferFrom lets a contract pull your tokens, but changing a non-zero allowance is racy: a spender watching the mempool can spend the old allowance then the new one. ERC-20 advises clients to set an allowance to zero before another non-zero value. SafeERC20 wraps transfer calls that return false or no value, and forceApprove supports tokens that require the zero-first approval sequence.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/SafeApprove.sol that pulls a token via SafeERC20 and uses forceApprove with a token that requires zero-first approval, with test/phase04/SafeApprove.t.sol using non-returning transfer and zero-first approval mocks. Done when: forge test proves typed transfer fails on the empty return while SafeERC20 succeeds, and forceApprove sets the zero-first token's allowance. Threat: forceApprove solves token-call compatibility, not the spender race when replacing a live allowance; prefer allowance deltas or revoke and account for already-spent value.

requirements.purpose: Explain the zero-first mitigation when replacing an existing ERC-20 allowance

options.title: ERC-20 approve Specification
options.scope: Section approve, including its client guidance note
options.why: The canonical ERC states overwrite semantics and places the zero-before-nonzero mitigation in client guidance rather than requiring token contracts to enforce it.

requirements.purpose: Use SafeERC20 for false-returning, no-returning, and zero-first approval tokens

options.title: OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 API
options.scope: Section SafeERC20 functions safeTransfer, safeTransferFrom, and forceApprove
options.why: The official current API defines empty-return handling and forceApprove's exact zero-first compatibility role.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-165 interface detection
proposedTopics.description: ERC-165 lets a contract advertise which interfaces it implements via supportsInterface(bytes4), where the id is the XOR of the interface's function selectors. ERC-721 and ERC-1155 require ERC-165 support, so declaring it correctly lets integrations discover their interface shape. It is only a self-declaration, though — a contract can claim support it does not honor.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Introspectable.sol overriding supportsInterface for a custom interface, with test/phase04/Introspectable.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves supportsInterface returns true for the declared interface id and the ERC-165 id (0x01ffc9a7) and false for 0xffffffff. Threat: interface-detection spoofing — supportsInterface is a claim, not a proof; still guard the actual calls.

requirements.purpose: Calculate, publish, and validate ERC-165 interface identifiers

options.title: ERC-165: Standard Interface Detection
options.scope: Sections How Interfaces are Identified through How to Detect if a Contract Implements any Given Interface
options.why: The final ERC supplies the XOR rule, required true and false identifiers, gas bound, and two-call detection procedure exercised by the build.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-721 non-fungible tokens
proposedTopics.description: ERC-721 gives each token a unique id with ownerOf/balanceOf, approve/setApprovalForAll, and safeTransferFrom, which calls onERC721Received on contract recipients and reverts on an invalid response. tokenURI is an optional metadata extension. The receiver callback is also an attack surface: minting via _safeMint hands control to the recipient mid-transaction.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/NFT.sol extending OZ ERC721 with a mint counter and tokenURI, plus test/phase04/NFT.t.sol including a malicious onERC721Received that re-enters mint. Done when: forge test proves ownerOf tracks transfers and the reentrant mint is stopped by CEI or a guard. Threat: onERC721Received reentrancy during _safeMint, and setApprovalForAll phishing that drains a whole collection.

requirements.purpose: Implement ERC-721 ownership, approvals, safe transfer, and optional metadata correctly

options.title: ERC-721: Non-Fungible Token Standard
options.scope: Section Specification, including ERC721, ERC721TokenReceiver, and metadata interfaces
options.why: The canonical final ERC defines ownership, operator approvals, receiver acceptance checks, ERC-165 identifiers, and the optional tokenURI extension.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-1155 multi-token standard
proposedTopics.description: ERC-1155 holds many token types — fungible and non-fungible — in one contract, with balanceOf(account,id), balanceOfBatch, and safeBatchTransferFrom for gas-efficient multi-transfers. Its optional metadata extension substitutes each token id into a shared {id} URI template, and contract recipients must return the required onERC1155Received or batch acceptance value.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/GameItems.sol extending OZ ERC1155 with a batch mint of several ids, plus test/phase04/GameItems.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves balanceOfBatch returns the minted amounts and a batch transfer updates every id atomically. Threat: receiver-callback reentrancy via onERC1155Received/Batch — apply CEI and nonReentrant on state-changing paths.

requirements.purpose: Implement multi-token batch accounting, metadata substitution, and receiver acceptance checks

options.title: ERC-1155: Multi Token Standard
options.scope: Sections ERC-1155 Token Receiver, Safe Transfer Rules, and Metadata
options.why: The canonical final ERC defines atomic batch semantics, required receiver magic values, event rules, and lowercase zero-padded {id} substitution.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-4626 tokenized vaults
proposedTopics.description: ERC-4626 standardizes a vault as an ERC-20 share token over one underlying asset: deposit/mint add assets for shares, withdraw/redeem do the reverse, while convert, preview, max, and totalAssets expose distinct integration views. Conversion formulas are implementation-defined, but the standard mandates method-specific rounding: outputs to users round down, required inputs round up, and both convert methods round down.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Vault.sol extending OZ ERC4626 over a mock asset, plus test/phase04/Vault.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves deposit mints shares, redeem returns assets, and convertToShares rounds down (assets→shares) so a user can never round up free value. Threat: first-depositor inflation via a direct donation to totalAssets — see the dedicated inflation-attack leaf.

requirements.purpose: Distinguish vault convert, preview, max, and state-changing methods and apply their required rounding directions

options.title: ERC-4626: Tokenized Vaults
options.why: The canonical final ERC defines each integration view and its asymmetric rounding contract without prescribing one exchange-rate formula.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-4626 inflation attack & virtual shares
proposedTopics.description: A naive empty ERC-4626 vault can be manipulated when an attacker deposits a tiny amount, then donates assets directly: the exchange rate rises and a later depositor can round to zero shares. OpenZeppelin's implementation includes virtual assets and shares in the conversion and lets _decimalsOffset() raise share precision; the virtual terms capture part of the donation, making the attack unprofitable even at offset zero and increasingly wasteful at larger offsets.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase04/InflationAttack.sol reproduce the donate-and-round exploit against a naive vault, then defend with OZ's virtual assets and shares at offset zero and a positive _decimalsOffset, with test/phase04/InflationAttack.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the naive attack is profitable, while forcing the defended vault's victim to zero shares costs the attacker at least the victim deposit at offset zero and orders of magnitude more with a positive offset. Threat: the defense makes theft unprofitable but cannot prevent a sufficiently funded attacker from griefing a depositor.

requirements.purpose: Reproduce donation-driven share inflation and quantify the virtual-offset defense

options.title: OpenZeppelin ERC-4626 Guide
options.scope: Sections Security concern: Inflation attack and Defending with a virtual offset
options.why: The official current guide derives the donation attack and shows how virtual assets, virtual shares, and decimals offset change attacker loss.

proposedTopics.title: delegatecall & the proxy pattern
proposedTopics.description: A proxy stores state and forwards calls via delegatecall to an implementation, so the implementation's code runs with the proxy's address, storage, balance, msg.sender, and msg.value. Changing the implementation can upgrade logic without moving proxy state. Because delegated code reads and writes the proxy's slots, successive implementations must preserve the established storage layout.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/MinimalProxy.sol — a fallback that delegatecalls a stored implementation — plus a LogicV1/LogicV2 pair and test/phase04/MinimalProxy.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves state set through the proxy survives an implementation swap and the swapped logic runs against the same storage. Threat: storage collision between proxy and logic, and delegatecall to an untrusted implementation that can overwrite or drain proxy state.

requirements.purpose: Trace delegated calldata, return data, caller/value, and proxy storage context

options.title: Solidity delegatecall and Libraries
options.why: The language reference defines whose address, storage, balance, msg.sender, and msg.value apply under delegatecall.

proposedTopics.title: ERC-1967 proxy storage slots
proposedTopics.description: ERC-1967 standardizes compiler-unallocated slots for a proxy's implementation, optional admin, and beacon. The implementation slot is bytes32(uint256(keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation')) - 1). Standard slots avoid accidental clashes with ordinary Solidity layout and let clients such as block explorers discover proxy metadata.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase04/Erc1967Slots.sol write to the implementation slot with sstore in assembly and read it back, plus test/phase04/Erc1967Slots.t.sol using vm.load. Done when: forge test proves the value read at keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation')-1 matches what you stored. Threat: slot collision — a proxy that parks its implementation pointer at slot 0 lets logic variables overwrite it.

requirements.purpose: Derive and inspect standardized implementation, beacon, and admin slots

options.title: ERC-1967: Proxy Storage Slots
options.why: The canonical final ERC gives all three constants, event expectations, client-discovery role, and collision rationale.

proposedTopics.title: Transparent proxy pattern
proposedTopics.description: The Transparent proxy handles selector clashes by routing on the caller: non-admin callers are delegated even when calldata matches the upgrade selector, while the admin can upgrade but cannot fall back to implementation functions. In OpenZeppelin v5 each proxy deploys an associated ProxyAdmin whose address is immutable in the proxy; ProxyAdmin ownership controls upgrades.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: deploy contracts/phase04 logic behind OZ's TransparentUpgradeableProxy + ProxyAdmin in a forge script/test test/phase04/Transparent.t.sol, then upgrade it. Done when: forge test proves a non-admin call reaches the logic, an admin-initiated upgrade swaps the implementation, and state persists across the upgrade. Threat: admin-key compromise (full upgrade power) and function-selector clash if you bypass the transparent routing.

requirements.purpose: Deploy and upgrade an OpenZeppelin v5 transparent proxy through its associated ProxyAdmin

options.title: OpenZeppelin TransparentUpgradeableProxy API
options.why: The official current API defines caller-dependent routing, the per-proxy associated ProxyAdmin, its ownership, and the v5 upgradeAndCall surface.

proposedTopics.title: UUPS proxy pattern
proposedTopics.description: UUPS puts the upgrade mechanism in the implementation behind an ERC1967Proxy. OpenZeppelin's UUPSUpgradeable exposes upgradeToAndCall, requires an access-restricted _authorizeUpgrade override, and checks the new implementation's ERC-1822 storage-slot compatibility. Removing upgradeability still requires an intentional or custom bypass of that safety check.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/CounterUUPS.sol (UUPSUpgradeable + onlyOwner _authorizeUpgrade) behind an ERC1967Proxy, plus test/phase04/UUPS.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves an unauthorized upgradeToAndCall reverts, an owner upgrade succeeds, state persists, and the current OZ compatibility check rejects a non-UUPS implementation. Threat: unprotected _authorizeUpgrade lets anyone upgrade; deliberately bypassing the ERC-1822 check can remove future upgradeability.

requirements.purpose: Authorize and compatibility-check upgrades performed by an implementation behind ERC1967Proxy

options.title: OpenZeppelin UUPSUpgradeable API
options.scope: Sections UUPS overview and UUPSUpgradeable functions onlyProxy, proxiableUUID, upgradeToAndCall, and _authorizeUpgrade
options.why: The official current API defines execution-context guards, mandatory authorization, and the ERC-1822 compatibility check that prevents accidental loss of upgradeability.

proposedTopics.title: Beacon proxy pattern
proposedTopics.description: A BeaconProxy gets its implementation from a shared UpgradeableBeacon, so one beacon upgrade changes the implementation used by every attached proxy while each proxy keeps independent state. In OpenZeppelin v5 the beacon address is immutable in each proxy, and the beacon's owner controls the fleet-wide implementation pointer.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/BeaconFactory.sol deploying multiple BeaconProxy instances against one UpgradeableBeacon, plus test/phase04/Beacon.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves upgrading the beacon changes the logic seen by all deployed proxies at once while their individual state is untouched. Threat: single-beacon compromise upgrades the entire fleet — guard beacon ownership as tightly as the funds.

requirements.purpose: Upgrade several state-isolated BeaconProxy instances through one controlled beacon

options.title: OpenZeppelin Beacon Proxy API
options.why: The official current API defines immutable beacon attachment, per-call implementation lookup, initialization, and owner-controlled fleet upgrades.

proposedTopics.title: Diamond pattern (EIP-2535)
proposedTopics.description: ERC-2535 defines a multi-facet proxy: a diamond maps function selectors to facet contracts and changes that mapping through diamondCut. Facet code executes by delegatecall against shared diamond storage. The standard describes Diamond Storage as one collision-avoidance approach, using a struct at a chosen namespaced slot; careful selector and storage discipline is essential.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/diamond/ with a Diamond, DiamondCutFacet, and two feature facets using Diamond Storage, plus test/phase04/Diamond.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a diamondCut adds a facet, calls route to the right facet by selector, and two facets read/write independent namespaced storage. Threat: selector clash between facets and storage-namespace collision corrupting unrelated facet state.

requirements.purpose: Add selector-routed facets and isolate their state in shared diamond storage

options.scope: Sections Specification, Adding/Replacing/Removing Functions, Storage, and Security Considerations
options.why: The canonical final ERC defines diamondCut actions and events, loupe introspection, delegatecall routing, and Diamond Storage as a collision-avoidance technique.

proposedTopics.title: Storage layout for upgrades
proposedTopics.description: Because a new implementation reads the proxy's existing storage, an upgrade must not reorder, remove, insert before, or change the type of established variables; safe additions go at the end. Storage gaps can reserve slots in upgradeable base contracts, while OpenZeppelin Contracts Upgradeable v5 uses ERC-7201 namespaced storage. Unsafe layout changes make the new code reinterpret existing bytes.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in contracts/phase04/LayoutV1.sol / LayoutV2.sol demonstrate a safe append and a deliberately-broken reorder, with test/phase04/Layout.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the appended-variable V2 preserves V1 state while the reordered V2 mis-reads it (values collide). Threat: storage collision on reorder/insert, or evolving a base without reserved gaps or an ERC-7201 namespace.

requirements.purpose: Classify safe and unsafe storage-layout changes, including base-contract evolution

options.title: OpenZeppelin Writing Upgradeable Contracts
options.scope: Sections Modifying Your Contracts, Storage Gaps, and Namespaced Storage Layout
options.why: The official upgrades guide gives invalid reorder/type/insert/remove cases and distinguishes storage gaps from ERC-7201 namespaced storage used in v5.

proposedTopics.title: Initializers & _disableInitializers
proposedTopics.description: Proxy instances do not receive state written by an implementation constructor, so upgradeable setup goes in an initializer and explicitly invokes parent initializers. Initializable supplies initializer and versioned reinitializer guards. The implementation's own constructor should call _disableInitializers() so an attacker cannot initialize and take over the otherwise unused implementation instance.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/InitializableLogic.sol with an initializer, _disableInitializers() in the constructor, and a reinitializer(2), plus test/phase04/Initializer.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves initialize runs once (a second call reverts), the implementation itself cannot be initialized, and reinitializer(2) runs exactly once. Threat: an unprotected proxy initializer or an unlocked implementation can be taken over by the first caller.

requirements.purpose: Initialize proxy storage once, compose parent initializers, and lock the implementation instance

options.title: OpenZeppelin Writing Upgradeable Contracts
options.scope: Sections Initializers, Initializing the Implementation Contract, and Validating Initializers
options.why: The official upgrades guide defines initializer guards, explicit parent initialization, reinitializer validation limits, and the _disableInitializers constructor pattern.

proposedTopics.title: Ownable (OZ v5)
proposedTopics.description: Ownable gives a contract one privileged owner and an onlyOwner modifier, with transferOwnership and renounceOwnership. In OpenZeppelin v5 its constructor takes an explicit initialOwner and rejects address(0). Renouncing sets the owner to the zero address and disables onlyOwner functionality, so both deployment ownership and renunciation require care.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Owned5.sol extending OZ v5 Ownable with an onlyOwner setter, plus test/phase04/Owned5.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves the constructor sets initialOwner, a non-owner call reverts with OwnableUnauthorizedAccount, and renounceOwnership leaves owner == address(0). Threat: single-key compromise = full control, and renouncing to address(0) permanently disables every admin path.

requirements.purpose: Set, enforce, transfer, and deliberately renounce a single privileged owner

options.scope: Section Ownable constructor, onlyOwner, transferOwnership, renounceOwnership, errors, and events
options.why: The official v5 API defines explicit nonzero initial ownership, custom unauthorized errors, and loss of onlyOwner access after renunciation.

proposedTopics.title: Role-based access control
proposedTopics.description: OpenZeppelin AccessControl uses bytes32 roles, onlyRole checks, and per-role admin relationships. DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is initially its own admin and administers other roles, making it especially sensitive. AccessControlDefaultAdminRules constrains that role to one account and adds a delayed two-step transfer.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Roled.sol with an explicit DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE holder plus separate MINTER_ROLE and PAUSER_ROLE accounts, with test/phase04/Roled.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves a minter can mint but not pause, the role admin can revoke MINTER_ROLE, and an unauthorized call reverts with AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount. Threat: a missing onlyRole modifier or an over-broad DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE collapses least-privilege back to one god key.

requirements.purpose: Separate capabilities into administered roles and protect the default admin

options.why: The official guide demonstrates role identifiers, onlyRole, grant/revoke administration, DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE risk, and the recommended delayed two-step AccessControlDefaultAdminRules extension.

proposedTopics.title: Two-step ownership transfer
proposedTopics.description: Single-step transferOwnership immediately sends control to the supplied address. Ownable2Step instead records a pendingOwner, and ownership moves only when that address calls acceptOwnership. This prevents completing a transfer to an address that cannot perform the acceptance, though the current owner must still manage or replace a mistaken pending transfer.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: implement contracts/phase04/Owned2Step.sol extending Ownable2Step with a constructor that forwards initialOwner to Ownable, plus test/phase04/Owned2Step.t.sol. Done when: forge test proves transferOwnership only sets pendingOwner (owner unchanged), acceptOwnership from the pending address completes the move, and acceptance from any other address reverts. Threat: single-step transfer to a wrong/uncontrolled address = irreversible loss of admin.

requirements.purpose: Require the nominated owner to accept before ownership changes

proposedPrompts.promptText: Name the core ERC-20 functions and one way a real token can break code that assumes 'standard' behaviour.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: totalSupply, balanceOf, transfer, transferFrom, approve, allowance (+ Transfer/Approval events). Pitfall: some tokens don't return the bool the spec mandates (old USDT), and fee-on-transfer/rebasing tokens deliver a different amount than requested — always use SafeERC20 and measure balance deltas.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Explain the ERC-20 approval race and what SafeERC20 does and does not solve.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: If an owner replaces allowance N with M, the spender can spend N before the update and later spend M. SafeERC20 handles false or empty returns; forceApprove handles tokens that require zero before non-zero, but neither makes separate owner transactions race-free. Prefer allowance deltas where applicable, or revoke and wait while accounting for value already spent.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Use SafeERC20 to set an allowance on a token that requires zero before non-zero approval.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: token.forceApprove(spender, newAmount); forceApprove performs the compatibility sequence for tokens that require zero before a new non-zero approval. Avoid presenting two forceApprove calls as necessary, and remember that zero-first reduces token compatibility problems but cannot make two separate pending transactions atomic.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How is an ERC-165 interface id computed, and what does supportsInterface actually guarantee?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The id is the XOR of the interface's 4-byte function selectors; supportsInterface(id) returns whether the contract claims to implement it. Pitfall: it's a self-declaration, not a proof — a contract can return true and still not honour the behaviour, so keep guarding the real calls.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does safeTransferFrom call onERC721Received, and what risk does that introduce during _safeMint?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It checks a contract recipient can handle NFTs (returns the magic selector) so tokens don't get stranded. Pitfall: the callback hands execution to the recipient mid-transaction — if _safeMint runs before state is finalized, the recipient can re-enter and mint again. Follow checks-effects-interactions or add nonReentrant.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Ethernaut-style: exploit a mint function that calls _safeMint before updating its per-address mint cap.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Deploy a contract whose onERC721Received calls mint again; because the cap is written after _safeMint, the callback sees the stale count and mints past the limit. Fix by writing the count before the external _safeMint (CEI) or guarding with nonReentrant.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does ERC-1155 do that needing a separate ERC-20/721 deployment per asset would not?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: One contract holds many token types addressed by id, with batch balance queries and safeBatchTransferFrom for atomic multi-transfers; the optional metadata extension uses an {id}-templated URI. Pitfall: recipients' acceptance callbacks are a reentrancy surface — finalize application state before the external callback.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Which way must ERC-4626 conversions and previews round?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Both convert methods round down. User outputs round down: previewDeposit returns no more shares than deposit and previewRedeem no more assets than redeem. Required inputs round up: previewMint returns no fewer assets and previewWithdraw no fewer shares. The standard does not require every vault's conversion estimate to equal totalAssets/totalSupply.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Walk through the ERC-4626 first-depositor inflation attack and OZ's defense.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Against a naive empty vault, an attacker deposits dust then donates assets, raising the rate until a victim deposit rounds to zero shares. OpenZeppelin includes virtual assets and shares; these capture part of the donation, so even offset zero makes the attack unprofitable. A positive _decimalsOffset increases precision and makes dilution increasingly wasteful.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Practice the inflation/donation class of vault bug on a wargame vault.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Reproduce it: deposit a dust amount, donate directly to inflate the share price, then let a victim deposit and round to zero shares. Then patch with virtual-offset shares and prove the exploit no longer profits. Damn Vulnerable DeFi has share/price-manipulation challenges in this family.

proposedPrompts.promptText: In a proxy, whose storage does the implementation's code modify, and what must the two contracts agree on?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: delegatecall runs the implementation's code in the PROXY's storage context (msg.sender/msg.value preserved), so all state lives in the proxy. They must agree exactly on storage layout. Pitfall: if the proxy stores its implementation pointer at a slot the logic also uses, a write collides and can brick or hijack the proxy — hence ERC-1967's reserved slots.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does ERC-1967 store the implementation address at keccak256('eip1967.proxy.implementation') - 1 instead of slot 0?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Sequential variable layout starts at slot 0 and grows up, so a pseudo-random high slot is astronomically unlikely to collide with the logic contract's variables, keeping the pointer safe. The '- 1' avoids the address being a known keccak preimage. Pitfall: rolling your own proxy with the pointer at slot 0 invites a storage collision.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What problem does the Transparent proxy solve, and how?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The selector-clash problem: proxy and implementation functions can share four-byte selectors. Transparent routing delegates every non-admin call, while the admin may upgrade but cannot fall back to implementation functions. In OpenZeppelin v5 the associated ProxyAdmin address is immutable; its owner holds the upgrade authority.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Where does UUPS put upgrade logic, and what must protect and preserve it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: UUPSUpgradeable puts upgradeToAndCall in the implementation behind ERC1967Proxy. _authorizeUpgrade must restrict callers, and OpenZeppelin checks proxiableUUID compatibility before installing the new implementation. A custom or deliberately bypassed check can still remove upgradeability; the current default rejects a plain non-UUPS implementation.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Legacy Ethernaut Motorbike: how did an unlocked implementation enable the historical pre-EIP-6780 bricking path?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The attacker initialized the implementation directly, gained its upgrade authority, then made it delegatecall code containing SELFDESTRUCT, historically deleting the implementation and leaving the proxy with no code target. _disableInitializers() prevents the takeover. Current EIP-6780 SELFDESTRUCT semantics no longer generally delete old contract code, so treat the destruction step as historical.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a Beacon proxy let you upgrade thousands of instances at once, and what's the trade-off?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Each proxy reads its implementation from a shared UpgradeableBeacon rather than storing it; upgrading the beacon once changes the logic for every proxy simultaneously, while each proxy keeps its own state. Pitfall: the beacon is a single fleet-wide upgrade point — compromising its owner upgrades (and can drain) every instance at once.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a Diamond route calls and keep facets from corrupting each other's storage?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: diamondCut maps each function selector to a facet; the fallback delegatecalls the facet owning the called selector, letting the system exceed 24 KB and upgrade per-facet. Facets share the proxy's storage, so each uses Diamond Storage — a struct at a namespaced slot keccak(unique string). Pitfall: two facets claiming the same selector, or reusing a storage namespace, corrupts state.

proposedPrompts.promptText: State the storage-layout rule for upgrades, then contrast storage gaps with ERC-7201 namespaces.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: For a sequential layout, append only: do not reorder, remove, insert before, or change existing variable types. A fixed __gap reserves base-contract slots and must shrink as the base consumes them. ERC-7201 instead isolates annotated namespaced structs; OpenZeppelin Contracts Upgradeable v5 uses this namespaced approach.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why can't upgradeable contracts use constructors, and why must the implementation call _disableInitializers()?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An implementation constructor writes only implementation state, not proxy state, so proxy setup goes in a guarded initialize function and must call parent initializers explicitly. The implementation constructor calls _disableInitializers() to stop anyone taking over that separate instance. Keep this distinct from the historical Parity library incident.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What changed about Ownable's constructor in OpenZeppelin v5, and what does renouncing ownership do?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: v5's constructor takes an explicit initialOwner (constructor(address initialOwner) Ownable(initialOwner)) and reverts on address(0), instead of v4's implicit msg.sender. renounceOwnership sets owner to address(0), permanently disabling every onlyOwner path. Pitfall: passing the wrong initialOwner at deploy, or renouncing while admin-only functions are still needed, is unrecoverable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does AccessControl enforce least privilege, and what is the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE risk?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Capabilities are separate bytes32 roles gated by onlyRole (MINTER_ROLE can't pause, etc.), granted/revoked independently via grantRole/revokeRole. Pitfall: DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE administers all roles, so one compromised admin can grant itself everything — protect it (AccessControlDefaultAdminRules for a delayed two-step admin handoff) and never leave a privileged function without its onlyRole check.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is Ownable2Step safer than single-step transferOwnership?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Single-step hands control to whatever address you pass — a typo or an address nobody controls loses the contract permanently. Ownable2Step records a pendingOwner and only completes when that address calls acceptOwnership, proving it exists and is controllable. Pitfall: even two-step can't save you if you set the pending owner to a contract that can't call acceptOwnership.
